1	// Offline route resolution: match a request against configured route prefixes
2	// and join the remainder onto the upstream base path without any network I/O.
3	package contractsentinel
4	
5	import (
6		"bytes"
7		"encoding/json"
8		"fmt"
9		"net/netip"
10		"net/url"
11		"sort"
12		"strings"
13	)
14	
15	// Route is one configured route: an id, accepted methods, a path prefix and
16	// the upstream URL requests on that route are forwarded to. An optional
17	// queryTransforms list rewrites the request query string after the route has
18	// been selected.
19	//
20	// QueryTransforms stays tag-less in the default (un)marshal sense: reading
21	// goes through Config.UnmarshalJSON, which decodes each route through the
22	// routeJSON raw mirror and validates the rules before they reach this field,
23	// and writing goes through Route.MarshalJSON, so the rules round-trip
24	// instead of being silently dropped (a plain json:"-" tag only omitted them
25	// on save).
26	type Route struct {
27		ID         string
28		Methods    []string
29		PathPrefix string
30		Upstream   string
31	
32		// QueryTransforms holds the validated rules. When it carries no rules
33		// the field is omitted on save, whether the source named no field or an
34		// explicit queryTransforms: [] — both are valid ways to write a route
35		// without rules, and ParseConfig accepts either.
36		QueryTransforms []*QueryTransform
37	}
38	
39	// pendingRoute is the read-side intermediate form of one route: the decoded
40	// basic fields alongside the still-unchecked raw queryTransforms value. It
41	// exists only inside the config reader, where the rules are validated against
42	// the route's 1-based position in check layer 3, and never becomes part of a
43	// finished Config — Route itself only ever carries the validated result, so
44	// no read path can observe a route that still holds unchecked rule text.
45	type pendingRoute struct {
46		route Route
47		// rawTransforms is the undecoded queryTransforms value, kept apart from
48		// the formal route data until checkQueryTransforms validates it.
49		rawTransforms json.RawMessage
50	}
51	
52	// MarshalJSON writes routes back in the shape ParseConfig accepts: the four
53	// basic fields in their canonical order, followed by queryTransforms when the
54	// route carries rules. A route without rules — whether the source omitted the
55	// field or named queryTransforms: [] — omits it, and ParseConfig accepts
56	// either spelling; the field is never written as null. The rules' order and
57	// literal strings are preserved byte for byte apart from JSON string
58	// escaping, so re-parsing the output and resolving yields the same routeId
59	// and upstreamURL.
60	func (r Route) MarshalJSON() ([]byte, error) {
61		type routeOut struct {
62			ID              string            `json:"id"`
63			Methods         []string          `json:"methods"`
64			PathPrefix      string            `json:"pathPrefix"`
65			Upstream        string            `json:"upstream"`
66			QueryTransforms []*QueryTransform `json:"queryTransforms,omitempty"`
67		}
68		return json.Marshal(routeOut{
69			ID:              r.ID,
70			Methods:         r.Methods,
71			PathPrefix:      r.PathPrefix,
72			Upstream:        r.Upstream,
73			QueryTransforms: r.QueryTransforms,
74		})
75	}
76	
77	// QueryTransform is one rule in a route's queryTransforms array: op is
78	// "set", "remove", "rename" or "copy"; name is matched against decoded
79	// parameter names, value (set only) is used literally, and to (rename and
80	// copy only) is the literal replacement or copy name.
81	type QueryTransform struct {
82		Op    string `json:"op"`
83		Name  string `json:"name"`
84		Value string `json:"value"`
85		To    string `json:"to"`
86	}
87	
88	// MarshalJSON renders each rule so the output satisfies the same constraints
89	// parseQueryTransforms enforces on input:
90	//   - set keeps "value" as a JSON string, including the empty string;
91	//   - remove emits only op and name (never value or to);
92	//   - rename and copy keep a non-empty "to" and never emit value.
93	//
94	// name, value and to are written as the literal strings read in — spaces,
95	// non-ASCII letters, '+' and '%' included — with only JSON string escaping,
96	// never query-string percent-encoding or decoding, so a re-read matches the
97	// same parameter names and applies the same literal values.
98	func (q *QueryTransform) MarshalJSON() ([]byte, error) {
99		switch q.Op {
100		case "set":
101			return json.Marshal(struct {
102				Op    string `json:"op"`
103				Name  string `json:"name"`
104				Value string `json:"value"`
105			}{q.Op, q.Name, q.Value})
106		case "rename", "copy":
107			return json.Marshal(struct {
108				Op   string `json:"op"`
109				Name string `json:"name"`
110				To   string `json:"to"`
111			}{q.Op, q.Name, q.To})
112		default:
113			// remove (and any op a validated config could never carry) writes
114			// neither value nor to, so the output cannot gain fields the reader
115			// rejects.
116			return json.Marshal(struct {
117				Op   string `json:"op"`
118				Name string `json:"name"`
119			}{q.Op, q.Name})
120		}
121	}
122	
123	// routeJSON mirrors Route but keeps every field raw: the basic fields are
124	// type-checked by decodeRoute with the route's position (and, when available,
125	// its id), so a wrong field type is reported on that route rather than as a
126	// generic JSON decode error, and queryTransforms can surface null, wrong
127	// types and malformed rules the same way.
128	type routeJSON struct {
129		ID              json.RawMessage `json:"id"`
130		Methods         json.RawMessage `json:"methods"`
131		PathPrefix      json.RawMessage `json:"pathPrefix"`
132		Upstream        json.RawMessage `json:"upstream"`
133		QueryTransforms json.RawMessage `json:"queryTransforms"`
134	}
135	
136	// decodeRoute type-checks and decodes one raw route object into its
137	// intermediate form: the basic fields land on the pending route, while the
138	// raw queryTransforms value travels alongside it, still unchecked, for check
139	// layer 3. loc is the route's 1-based location in its config (e.g.
140	// "route 2"). The element's JSON type is checked first: a null entry or any
141	// non-object value fails on the entry itself, naming the position, the
142	// required object type and the type actually received, instead of falling
143	// through to a missing-field error such as a missing id. Field type errors
144	// then carry that location and, when the route supplies a valid non-empty
145	// string id anywhere in its object (even after the offending field), that id.
146	// Missing fields stay silent here and are rejected later by validate, which
147	// preserves the existing missing-field behavior.
148	func decodeRoute(data []byte, loc string) (pendingRoute, *Failure) {
149		elem := bytes.TrimSpace(data)
150		if len(elem) == 0 || elem[0] != '{' {
151			return pendingRoute{}, failuref("invalid_config",
152				"%s: route entry must be an object, got %s", loc, jsonTypeName(elem))
153		}
154		var rj routeJSON
155		if err := json.Unmarshal(elem, &rj); err != nil {
156			// The element already parsed as one JSON value and starts with '{';
157			// an object that cannot be read is a syntax failure rather than a
158			// field type error.
159			return pendingRoute{}, failuref("invalid_config", "config is not valid JSON: %v", err)
160		}
161	
162		var pending pendingRoute
163		route := &pending.route
164		// Type-check id first so it can identify the route on an error in any
165		// later field regardless of object order. Only a valid non-empty JSON
166		// string becomes the label; a wrong-typed id is reported against the id
167		// field and never rendered (e.g. as a number or object) as the route's
168		// identity, so that error is located by position alone.
169		if !decodeStringField(rj.ID, &route.ID) {
170			return pendingRoute{}, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: id must be a string", loc)
171		}
172		label := loc
173		if route.ID != "" {
174			label = routeLabel(loc, route.ID)
175		}
176	
177		if f := decodeMethodsField(rj.Methods, label, &route.Methods); f != nil {
178			return pendingRoute{}, f
179		}
180		if f := decodeRouteStringField(rj.PathPrefix, label, "pathPrefix", &route.PathPrefix); f != nil {
181			return pendingRoute{}, f
182		}
183		if f := decodeRouteStringField(rj.Upstream, label, "upstream", &route.Upstream); f != nil {
184			return pendingRoute{}, f
185		}
186		pending.rawTransforms = rj.QueryTransforms
187		return pending, nil
188	}
189	
190	// decodeRouteStringField renders a route field's string type error with the
191	// route's position (and, when available, its id); the type decision itself is
192	// the shared decodeStringField. An absent field stays silent for the later
193	// required-field validation.
194	func decodeRouteStringField(raw json.RawMessage, label, field string, dst *string) *Failure {
195		if !decodeStringField(raw, dst) {
196			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s: %s must be a string", label, field)
197		}
198		return nil
199	}
200	
201	// decodeStringField type-checks a raw field that must hold a string. It is
202	// the one shared string-field decision used by both config and request
203	// decoding, so the absent / null / non-string / empty-string distinctions
204	// live in one place. It returns false only when the key is present with a
205	// non-string value (null included), which is always a field type error. An
206	// absent key leaves dst untouched, and a present string — the empty string
207	// included — is decoded into dst, so both reach the existing content checks
208	// unchanged.
209	func decodeStringField(raw json.RawMessage, dst *string) (isString bool) {
210		if len(raw) == 0 {
211			return true
212		}
213		return jsonString(raw, dst)
214	}
215	
216	// decodeMethodsField type-checks methods: it must be an array of strings
217	// when present. An absent field is left nil for later required-field
218	// validation; null or any non-array value fails the field, and a number,
219	// boolean, object or null entry fails with the offending entry's position.
220	func decodeMethodsField(raw json.RawMessage, label string, dst *[]string) *Failure {
221		if len(raw) == 0 {
222			return nil
223		}
224		body := bytes.TrimSpace(raw)
225		if string(body) == "null" || len(body) == 0 || body[0] != '[' {
226			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s: methods must be an array of strings", label)
227		}
228		var elems []json.RawMessage
229		if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &elems); err != nil {
230			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s: methods must be an array of strings", label)
231		}
232		methods := make([]string, 0, len(elems))
233		for i, elem := range elems {
234			var m string
235			if !jsonString(bytes.TrimSpace(elem), &m) {
236				return failuref("invalid_config", "%s: methods entry %d must be a string", label, i+1)
237			}
238			methods = append(methods, m)
239		}
240		*dst = methods
241		return nil
242	}
243	
244	// parseQueryTransforms decodes and validates the raw queryTransforms array
245	// of one route. loc identifies the route; rule errors additionally carry a
246	// 1-based rule index.
247	func parseQueryTransforms(raw json.RawMessage, loc, id string) ([]*QueryTransform, *Failure) {
248		body := strings.TrimSpace(string(raw))
249		if body == "null" {
250			return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: queryTransforms must not be null", routeLabel(loc, id))
251		}
252		var elems []json.RawMessage
253		if err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(body), &elems); err != nil {
254			return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: queryTransforms must be an array", routeLabel(loc, id))
255		}
256		transforms := make([]*QueryTransform, 0, len(elems))
257		for i, elem := range elems {
258			ruleLoc := fmt.Sprintf("%s, queryTransforms rule %d", routeLabel(loc, id), i+1)
259			if string(bytes.TrimSpace(elem)) == "null" {
260				return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: rule must not be null", ruleLoc)
261			}
262			var fields map[string]json.RawMessage
263			if err := json.Unmarshal(elem, &fields); err != nil {
264				return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: rule must be a JSON object", ruleLoc)
265			}
266	
267			qt := &QueryTransform{}
268			opRaw, ok := fields["op"]
269			switch {
270			case !ok:
271				return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: op is required", ruleLoc)
272			case !jsonString(opRaw, &qt.Op):
273				return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: op must be a string", ruleLoc)
274			case qt.Op != "set" && qt.Op != "remove" && qt.Op != "rename" && qt.Op != "copy":
275				return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: unknown op %q (only set, remove, rename and copy are supported)", ruleLoc, qt.Op)
276			}
277	
278			nameRaw, ok := fields["name"]
279			switch {
280			case !ok:
281				return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: name is required", ruleLoc)
282			case !jsonString(nameRaw, &qt.Name):
283				return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: name must be a non-empty string", ruleLoc)
284			case qt.Name == "":
285				return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: name must be a non-empty string", ruleLoc)
286			}
287	
288			valueRaw, hasValue := fields["value"]
289			toRaw, hasTo := fields["to"]
290			switch qt.Op {
291			case "set":
292				if !hasValue {
293					return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: set requires a string value", ruleLoc)
294				}
295				if !jsonString(valueRaw, &qt.Value) {
296					return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: value must be a string", ruleLoc)
297				}
298			case "remove":
299				if hasValue {
300					return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: remove must not include a value", ruleLoc)
301				}
302			case "rename":
303				if hasValue {
304					return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: rename must not include a value", ruleLoc)
305				}
306				switch {
307				case !hasTo:
308					return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: rename requires a non-empty string to", ruleLoc)
309				case !jsonString(toRaw, &qt.To):
310					return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: to must be a non-empty string", ruleLoc)
311				case qt.To == "":
312					return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: to must be a non-empty string", ruleLoc)
313				}
314			case "copy":
315				if hasValue {
316					return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: copy must not include a value", ruleLoc)
317				}
318				switch {
319				case !hasTo:
320					return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: copy requires a non-empty string to", ruleLoc)
321				case !jsonString(toRaw, &qt.To):
322					return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: to must be a non-empty string", ruleLoc)
323				case qt.To == "":
324					return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "%s: to must be a non-empty string", ruleLoc)
325				}
326			}
327			transforms = append(transforms, qt)
328		}
329		return transforms, nil
330	}
331	
332	// jsonString decodes raw into s and reports whether raw is a JSON string
333	// (null, numbers, objects and arrays fail).
334	func jsonString(raw json.RawMessage, s *string) bool {
335		if len(raw) == 0 || raw[0] != '"' {
336			return false
337		}
338		return json.Unmarshal(raw, s) == nil
339	}
340	
341	// routeLabel renders the human-readable route location, adding the id when
342	// the configuration supplied one.
343	func routeLabel(loc, id string) string {
344		if id != "" {
345			return fmt.Sprintf("%s (id %q)", loc, id)
346		}
347		return loc
348	}

350	// Config is the resolve configuration: a flat array of routes.
351	type Config struct {
352		Routes []Route `json:"routes"`
353	}
354	
355	// MarshalJSON writes the config back in the shape ParseConfig accepts. A
356	// non-nil empty (or nil) routes slice is emitted as "routes": [] rather than
357	// "routes": null, which ParseConfig would reject with invalid_config; the
358	// routes keep their parsed order and each route marshals through
359	// Route.MarshalJSON so its queryTransforms survive the save.
360	func (cfg *Config) MarshalJSON() ([]byte, error) {
361		routes := cfg.Routes
362		if routes == nil {
363			routes = []Route{}
364		}
365		return json.Marshal(struct {
366			Routes []Route `json:"routes"`
367		}{Routes: routes})
368	}
369	
370	// UnmarshalJSON runs check layers 1–3 of config reading (see ParseConfig for
371	// the full layer list and the error-selection rules): JSON syntax, then the
372	// document structure and basic field types, then the queryTransforms rules.
373	// Layer 4 (field contents) is Config.validate, run by ParseConfig after
374	// decoding. The routes are decoded one entry at a time from raw values, each
375	// type-checked against its 1-based position in this config, so a wrong field
376	// type is reported on the offending route (with its id when available)
377	// instead of as a generic JSON syntax failure, and configs parsed
378	// concurrently or interleaved in the same process cannot shift each other's
379	// route numbering. A broken JSON document fails the outer decode and is
380	// reported as a parse failure, without a guessed route position or field.
381	func (cfg *Config) UnmarshalJSON(data []byte) error {
382		read, err := readConfig(data)
383		if err != nil {
384			return err
385		}
386		*cfg = *read
387		return nil
388	}
389	
390	// readConfig runs check layers 1–3 and returns the configuration with every
391	// route's basic fields decoded and its queryTransforms validated. The
392	// intermediate pendingRoutes keep the unchecked rule text out of the
393	// returned Config; layer 4 (field contents) is Config.validate, run by
394	// ParseConfig.
395	func readConfig(data []byte) (*Config, error) {
396		// Layer 1: JSON syntax. A broken document is only ever a parse failure,
397		// reported without a guessed route position or field.
398		body, err := unmarshalJSONValue(data)
399		if err != nil {
400			return nil, err
401		}
402		// Layer 2: structure and basic field types.
403		if f := requireJSONObject(body, "invalid_config", "config", true); f != nil {
404			return nil, f
405		}
406		routes, err := decodeConfigRoutes(body)
407		if err != nil {
408			return nil, err
409		}
410		// Layer 3: query rewrite rules, checked only once every route's basic
411		// fields have the right type, so a type error on any route — earlier or
412		// later — is always reported before any rule error.
413		if f := checkQueryTransforms(routes); f != nil {
414			return nil, f
415		}
416		cfg := &Config{Routes: make([]Route, len(routes))}
417		for i := range routes {
418			cfg.Routes[i] = routes[i].route
419		}
420		return cfg, nil
421	}
422	
423	// decodeConfigRoutes is check layer 2: the top-level object is taken apart
424	// and every route entry is type-checked against its 1-based position. The
425	// routes field must hold an array when present — null is a type error here,
426	// never an absent field: a config that explicitly supplies routes must supply
427	// an array. A non-object entry (null included) fails on that entry before
428	// any field is inspected, and a wrong field type is reported on the offending
429	// route with its id when the route supplies a valid non-empty string id
430	// anywhere in its object. Each route's unchecked queryTransforms value
431	// travels in the returned pendingRoutes for layer 3.
432	func decodeConfigRoutes(body json.RawMessage) ([]pendingRoute, error) {
433		var fields map[string]json.RawMessage
434		if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &fields); err != nil {
435			return nil, err
436		}
437	
438		var rawRoutes []json.RawMessage
439		if raw, ok := fields["routes"]; ok {
440			elem := bytes.TrimSpace(raw)
441			if len(elem) == 0 || elem[0] != '[' {
442				return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "routes must be an array, got %s", jsonTypeName(elem))
443			}
444			if err := json.Unmarshal(elem, &rawRoutes); err != nil {
445				return nil, err
446			}
447		}
448	
449		routes := make([]pendingRoute, len(rawRoutes))
450		for i, entry := range rawRoutes {
451			route, f := decodeRoute(entry, fmt.Sprintf("route %d", i+1))
452			if f != nil {
453				return nil, f
454			}
455			routes[i] = route
456		}
457		return routes, nil
458	}
459	
460	// checkQueryTransforms is check layer 3: every route's raw queryTransforms
461	// value is decoded and validated against the route's 1-based position, in
462	// routes-array order, and the validated rules replace the pending raw value.
463	// It runs only after layer 2 has cleared every route, so a basic-field type
464	// error on any route — earlier or later — is always reported before any rule
465	// error, while within this layer the earliest route (and within it the
466	// earliest rule) wins.
467	func checkQueryTransforms(routes []pendingRoute) *Failure {
468		for i := range routes {
469			if len(routes[i].rawTransforms) == 0 {
470				continue // field absent
471			}
472			loc := fmt.Sprintf("route %d", i+1)
473			transforms, f := parseQueryTransforms(routes[i].rawTransforms, loc, routes[i].route.ID)
474			if f != nil {
475				return f
476			}
477			routes[i].route.QueryTransforms = transforms
478			routes[i].rawTransforms = nil
479		}
480		return nil
481	}
482	
483	// unmarshalJSONValue is the shared first step of parsing either input: it
484	// confirms the document is one syntactically valid JSON value, without
485	// judging its shape. It returns encoding/json's own error verbatim, so each
486	// caller keeps its existing handling (ParseConfig wraps a returned error just
487	// as Config.UnmarshalJSON returning it directly always has).
488	func unmarshalJSONValue(data []byte) (json.RawMessage, error) {
489		var doc json.RawMessage
490		if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &doc); err != nil {
491			return nil, err
492		}
493		return bytes.TrimSpace(doc), nil
494	}
495	
496	// requireJSONObject is the shared top-level shape check: a syntactically
497	// legal value that is not a JSON object is a structural error in the caller's
498	// code saying "<what> must be a JSON object", never a parse failure and never
499	// a guessed field or route position. Config errors additionally name the type
500	// actually received ("got <type>"); the request wording omits it.
501	func requireJSONObject(doc json.RawMessage, code, what string, nameType bool) *Failure {
502		if len(doc) == 0 || doc[0] != '{' {
503			if nameType {
504				return failuref(code, "%s must be a JSON object, got %s", what, jsonTypeName(doc))
505			}
506			return failuref(code, "%s must be a JSON object", what)
507		}
508		return nil
509	}

511	// Request is one resolution request: an HTTP method and a request target
512	// (path with an optional raw query string).
513	type Request struct {
514		Method string `json:"method"`
515		Target string `json:"target"`
516	}
517	
518	// Resolution is the successful result of matching a request.
519	type Resolution struct {
520		RouteID     string `json:"routeId"`
521		UpstreamURL string `json:"upstreamURL"`
522	}
523	
524	// Failure carries a stable machine-readable code and a human-readable reason.
525	type Failure struct {
526		Code       string   `json:"code"`
527		Reason     string   `json:"reason"`
528		Candidates []string `json:"candidates,omitempty"`
529	}
530	
531	func (f *Failure) Error() string { return f.Code + ": " + f.Reason }
532	
533	func failuref(code, format string, args ...any) *Failure {
534		return &Failure{Code: code, Reason: fmt.Sprintf(format, args...)}
535	}
536	
537	// ParseConfig parses and fully validates the route configuration. Reading
538	// checks the document in four layers, and the first layer that finds a
539	// problem decides which error is reported:
540	//
541	//  1. JSON syntax: a broken document is only ever a parse failure, reported
542	//     without a guessed route position or field.
543	//  2. Structure and basic field types: the top-level value must be an
544	//     object, routes must be an array of objects, and id, methods,
545	//     pathPrefix and upstream must carry their JSON types.
546	//  3. Query rewrite rules: each route's queryTransforms array and every rule
547	//     in it.
548	//  4. Field contents: a non-empty unique id, legal methods, an absolute
549	//     pathPrefix (with no direct space, C0 control byte or DEL — only
550	//     percent encoding may carry those) and a valid upstream
551	//     (Config.validate).
552	//
553	// Within one layer the earliest array position wins — routes by their
554	// position in the routes array and rules by their position in the route's
555	// queryTransforms array, never by id ordering or by the object field order.
556	// Layers 1–3 run in Config.UnmarshalJSON (so they also guard a plain
557	// json.Unmarshal into a Config); layer 4 runs here, after decoding. Every
558	// failure hands back no config at all, so a half-parsed configuration can
559	// never resolve a request.
560	func ParseConfig(data []byte) (*Config, *Failure) {
561		var cfg Config
562		if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &cfg); err != nil {
563			if f, ok := err.(*Failure); ok {
564				return nil, f
565			}
566			return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "config is not valid JSON: %v", err)
567		}
568		if f := cfg.validate(); f != nil {
569			return nil, f
570		}
571		return &cfg, nil
572	}
573	
574	// validate is check layer 4 (see ParseConfig): the field contents of every
575	// route, in routes-array order. It runs only after layers 1–3 have cleared
576	// the whole document, so any structure, field-type or rule error anywhere is
577	// reported before any content error.
578	func (cfg *Config) validate() *Failure {
579		seenIDs := make(map[string]int, len(cfg.Routes))
580		for i := range cfg.Routes {
581			route := &cfg.Routes[i]
582			loc := fmt.Sprintf("route %d", i+1)
583			if route.ID == "" {
584				return failuref("invalid_config", "%s: id must be non-empty", loc)
585			}
586			if first, ok := seenIDs[route.ID]; ok {
587				return failuref("invalid_config", "%s: duplicate id %q (already used by route %d)", loc, route.ID, first)
588			}
589			seenIDs[route.ID] = i + 1
590	
591			if len(route.Methods) == 0 {
592				return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): methods must be a non-empty array", loc, route.ID)
593			}
594			for _, method := range route.Methods {
595				switch {
596				case method == "":
597					return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): methods must not contain empty entries", loc, route.ID)
598				case method == "*":
599					// Wildcard matching any legal method.
600				case !isToken(method):
601					return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): invalid method %q", loc, route.ID, method)
602				}
603			}
604	
605			if f := validatePrefix(route.PathPrefix, loc, route.ID); f != nil {
606				return f
607			}
608			if f := validateUpstream(route.Upstream, loc, route.ID); f != nil {
609				return f
610			}
611		}
612		return nil
613	}
614	
615	func validatePrefix(prefix, loc, id string) *Failure {
616		switch {
617		case prefix == "" || prefix[0] != '/':
618			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): pathPrefix must start with /", loc, id)
619		case prefix != "/" && strings.HasSuffix(prefix, "/"):
620			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): pathPrefix must not end with / except for root", loc, id)
621		case strings.ContainsAny(prefix, "?#"):
622			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): pathPrefix must not contain a query string or fragment", loc, id)
623		case !validPercentEscapes(prefix):
624			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): pathPrefix contains an invalid percent escape", loc, id)
625		}
626		if f := validatePrefixDirectCharacters(prefix, loc, id); f != nil {
627			return f
628		}
629		return nil
630	}
631	
632	// validatePrefixDirectCharacters rejects a direct space or control byte in a
633	// pathPrefix: a direct ASCII space (U+0020), a C0 control byte (U+0000
634	// through U+001F) or DEL (U+007F) makes the whole configuration
635	// invalid_config, because a request target can never carry that character
636	// directly — ParseRequest rejects it before route selection — so such a
637	// prefix could never be hit by a legal request. The check is decided on the
638	// decoded configured string: writing the byte literally or spelling it as a
639	// JSON escape ("\n", "\t", or the backslash-u0020 space escape) decodes to
640	// the same byte and fails
641	// the same way. Bytes inside a well-formed percent escape are skipped
642	// without decoding, so "%20", "%09" and "%00" stay legal raw text and keep
643	// matching on the raw encoded form; the prefix is never trimmed, the byte is
644	// never stripped or percent-encoded on the user's behalf, and the rule is
645	// not widened to other Unicode content (e.g. Chinese characters). It runs in
646	// check layer 4 (Config.validate), after JSON syntax, structure and basic
647	// field types and the queryTransforms rules, in routes-array order like the
648	// other field-content checks, so a later route's bad queryTransforms rule or
649	// an earlier route's other content error keeps its existing precedence. The
650	// reason names the pathPrefix field, the route's 1-based position and valid
651	// non-empty id and the first offending character as U+XXXX.
652	func validatePrefixDirectCharacters(prefix, loc, id string) *Failure {
653		if c, ok := firstDirectRawCharacter(prefix); ok {
654			return failuref("invalid_config",
655				"%s (id %q): pathPrefix contains a character that must be percent-encoded: U+%04X is not allowed to appear directly in a pathPrefix (a request target may not carry it directly either, so no legal request could match this route; percent-encode it, e.g. %%20 for a space; the prefix is used exactly as configured and the byte is never stripped, trimmed or encoded on its behalf)",
656				loc, id, c)
657		}
658		return nil
659	}

661	// upstreamParts is the one shared reading of a raw upstream URL's address
662	// boundaries. Every field is a slice of the original bytes (nothing is
663	// copied, decoded or normalized), so validation and joining cannot disagree
664	// about where one part ends and the next begins:
665	//
666	//	scheme "://" [userinfo "@"] hostPort basePath
667	//
668	// authority runs from after "://" to the first path slash, and hostPort is
669	// the authority after its last '@', so colons in userinfo or the base path
670	// can never be read as part of an IPv6 host, while brackets, a port and a
671	// zone stay inside hostPort.
672	type upstreamParts struct {
673		raw       string // the upstream exactly as configured; every other field slices this
674		schemeEnd int    // index of the ':' in "://", or -1 when the scheme is absent
675		authority string // bytes between "://" and the first path slash (userinfo included)
676		hostPort  string // authority after the last '@' (host plus optional port)
677		basePath  string // from the first path slash to the end, or ""
678	}
679	
680	// splitUpstream applies the single boundary rule shared by the bracketed-host
681	// check, the unbracketed-IPv6 check and the final join. It never rejects
682	// anything on its own: a raw value without "://" comes back with schemeEnd
683	// set to -1 and empty parts, leaving the generic absolute-URL check to
684	// report it, exactly as the per-caller preamble used to.
685	func splitUpstream(raw string) upstreamParts {
686		p := upstreamParts{raw: raw, schemeEnd: -1}
687		i := strings.Index(raw, "://")
688		if i < 0 {
689			return p
690		}
691		p.schemeEnd = i
692		tail := raw[i+3:]
693		if j := strings.IndexByte(tail, '/'); j >= 0 {
694			p.authority = tail[:j]
695			p.basePath = tail[j:]
696		} else {
697			p.authority = tail
698		}
699		// Any userinfo precedes the host and ends at the last '@'; that boundary
700		// is what keeps a userinfo colon out of the IPv6-host checks.
701		p.hostPort = p.authority
702		if k := strings.LastIndexByte(p.authority, '@'); k >= 0 {
703			p.hostPort = p.authority[k+1:]
704		}
705		return p
706	}
707	
708	func validateUpstream(raw, loc, id string) *Failure {
709		if strings.ContainsAny(raw, "?#") {
710			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): upstream must not contain a query string or fragment", loc, id)
711		}
712		// Validate the host's IP-literal spelling against the raw string before
713		// url.Parse: square brackets are the IP-literal marker, so whatever they
714		// enclose must be a legal IPv6 address (full, compressed or IPv4-tail,
715		// zone included) rather than a name or an IPv4 address, and an IPv6
716		// literal may never appear without that pair of brackets. Both checks and
717		// the later join read the same splitUpstream boundaries, which keeps the
718		// rules independent of url.Parse's parser strictness and lets the reason
719		// name the field and the actual problem instead of surfacing a generic URL
720		// parse error (an unbracketed literal otherwise reaches the user as a
721		// misleading "invalid port" complaint).
722		p := splitUpstream(raw)
723		if f := validateBracketedUpstreamHost(p, loc, id); f != nil {
724			return f
725		}
726		if f := validateUnbracketedUpstreamHost(p, loc, id); f != nil {
727			return f
728		}
729		if f := validateUpstreamHostPresent(p, loc, id); f != nil {
730			return f
731		}
732		if f := validateUpstreamBasePathSpace(p, loc, id); f != nil {
733			return f
734		}
735		u, err := url.Parse(raw)
736		if err != nil {
737			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): upstream is not a valid URL: %v", loc, id, err)
738		}
739		if u.Scheme != "http" && u.Scheme != "https" {
740			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): upstream must be an absolute http or https URL", loc, id)
741		}
742		if u.Host == "" {
743			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): upstream must include a host", loc, id)
744		}
745		return nil
746	}

748	// validateUpstreamHostPresent enforces on the split raw boundaries that the
749	// authority carries a non-empty host:
750	//
751	//	scheme "://" [userinfo "@"] host [":" port] [basePath]
752	//
753	// The check is needed because url.Parse treats a leading colon as a port
754	// separator with an empty hostname: it reads "http://:8080/base" with
755	// Host==":8080" and Hostname()=="" instead of rejecting it, so a check on
756	// u.Host alone lets the address through and the joined upstream is emitted
757	// without a host. The raw decision therefore fails every hostPort that is
758	// empty or begins with the port colon — an empty authority
759	// ("http:///base"), an authority reduced to userinfo ("http://u@/base"),
760	// a bare port with or without digits ("http://:8080/base",
761	// "https://:8443", "http://:/base") and any of those after userinfo
762	// ("https://user:p%40ss@:8443/v1"). Neither userinfo, the port nor a base
763	// path can fill the host slot, no default address is ever substituted, and
764	// a host that is simply followed by an empty port ("http://host:/base")
765	// stays accepted: its hostPort begins with the host, not the separator.
766	// Like the bracket rules this is a content error in a syntactically valid
767	// JSON document — the reason names the route's 1-based position, its id and
768	// the upstream field and says the upstream is missing a host, never that
769	// the JSON is broken or that an IPv6 literal needs brackets.
770	func validateUpstreamHostPresent(p upstreamParts, loc, id string) *Failure {
771		if p.schemeEnd < 0 {
772			return nil // no scheme: the generic absolute-URL check reports this
773		}
774		hostPort := p.hostPort
775		if hostPort != "" && hostPort[0] != ':' {
776			return nil
777		}
778		return failuref("invalid_config",
779			"%s: upstream %q is missing a host: the address must carry a non-empty host before any port (e.g. \"http://example.com:8080/base\"); a port cannot serve as the host, and userinfo or a base path cannot fill the host in either; no default host is added",
780			routeLabel(loc, id), p.raw)
781	}
782	
783	// validateUpstreamBasePathSpace rejects a direct ASCII space (U+0020) in the
784	// upstream base path — inside a path segment, beside a slash or at the end,
785	// it is all the same error. Only percent encoding may carry a space there:
786	// "%20" is legal path content and is never decoded first, so an encoded
787	// space stays accepted while the literal byte is rejected. The check reads
788	// the same splitUpstream base-path boundaries the join uses, so a space that
789	// would reach upstreamURL can never pass validation. It is decided on the
790	// decoded configured string (a " " JSON escape decodes to the same
791	// byte), only the ASCII space is rejected — the rule is not widened to other
792	// Unicode whitespace — and the address is judged exactly as configured: the
793	// space is never stripped, the path never trimmed and the byte never
794	// re-encoded on the user's behalf. The reason names the route's 1-based
795	// position, its id and the upstream field; like the host rules this is a
796	// content error in a syntactically valid JSON document, never a JSON parse
797	// failure.
798	func validateUpstreamBasePathSpace(p upstreamParts, loc, id string) *Failure {
799		if p.schemeEnd < 0 {
800			return nil // no scheme: the generic absolute-URL check reports this
801		}
802		if !strings.ContainsRune(p.basePath, ' ') {
803			return nil
804		}
805		return failuref("invalid_config",
806			"%s: upstream base path contains an unencoded space (U+0020): a space in the upstream address must be percent-encoded as %%20 in the configuration; the address is used exactly as configured and the space is never stripped, the path never trimmed and the byte never encoded on its behalf",
807			routeLabel(loc, id))
808	}
809	
810	// validateBracketedUpstreamHost checks the split raw upstream's authority for
811	// an IP literal in square brackets: brackets are reserved for an IPv6 (or
812	// future IP-version) literal, so their content must parse as an IPv6 address
813	// — full form, compressed form or an IPv6 address with an embedded IPv4
814	// tail — and the brackets must wrap the whole host exactly once:
815	//
816	//	"[" IPv6 "]" [ ":" *DIGIT ]
817	//
818	// A port, userinfo and a percent-encoded zone ("%25eth0") are allowed and
819	// never alter the literal's bytes; an empty pair of brackets, a plain
820	// hostname such as "[not-an-ip]", a bare IPv4 address such as
821	// "[127.0.0.1]", a malformed IPv6 literal, a missing closing bracket, a
822	// second bracket group such as "[::1][::2]", a stray closing bracket or any
823	// other text between the closing bracket and the start of the base path
824	// (including junk around the port such as "[::1]:80a" or "[::1]x]:80") are
825	// rejected — a legal first literal never legitimizes trailing content. The
826	// reason names the route, its id and the upstream field. This is a content
827	// error in a syntactically valid JSON document, never a JSON parse failure,
828	// and the rule is enforced here on the raw bytes rather than left to
829	// url.Parse's parser strictness.
830	func validateBracketedUpstreamHost(p upstreamParts, loc, id string) *Failure {
831		if p.schemeEnd < 0 {
832			return nil // no scheme: the generic absolute-URL check reports this
833		}
834		hostPort := p.hostPort
835	
836		if !strings.ContainsAny(hostPort, "[]") {
837			return nil // ordinary reg-name (domain) or bare IPv4 host stays as-is
838		}
839		label := routeLabel(loc, id)
840		if !strings.HasPrefix(hostPort, "[") {
841			return failuref("invalid_config",
842				"%s: upstream bracketed host must be a single '[' IPv6 address ']' pair: '[' may only open the host", label)
843		}
844		closeBracket := strings.IndexByte(hostPort, ']')
845		if closeBracket < 0 {
846			return failuref("invalid_config",
847				"%s: upstream bracketed host must be a valid IPv6 address but the closing ']' is missing", label)
848		}
849		literal := hostPort[1:closeBracket]
850		// The zone delimiter is percent-encoded in the URL ("%25"); decode the
851		// literal's escapes once so netip sees "fe80::1%eth0" while every other
852		// byte keeps its original spelling.
853		decoded, err := url.PathUnescape(literal)
854		if err != nil {
855			return invalidBracketedHost(label, literal)
856		}
857		addr, err := netip.ParseAddr(decoded)
858		if err != nil || !addr.Is6() {
859			// ParseAddr accepts a bare IPv4 address; brackets may only carry
860			// IPv6, so "[127.0.0.1]" is rejected even though it is a valid IP.
861			return invalidBracketedHost(label, literal)
862		}
863		// The one closing bracket ends the host: the rest of the authority may
864		// be empty or the optional port the generic parser already allows
865		// (":" followed by digits, an empty port included). A repeated bracket
866		// group, a stray ']', or any other text before, beside or after a port
867		// fails here even though the first literal was valid — the brackets
868		// must enclose the whole host exactly once.
869		suffix := hostPort[closeBracket+1:]
870		switch {
871		case suffix == "":
872			return nil
873		case strings.ContainsAny(suffix, "[]"):
874			return invalidBracketedHostShape(label, suffix)
875		case suffix[0] != ':':
876			return invalidBracketedHostShape(label, suffix)
877		}
878		port := suffix[1:]
879		for i := 0; i < len(port); i++ {
880			if port[i] < '0' || port[i] > '9' {
881				return invalidBracketedHostShape(label, suffix)
882			}
883		}
884		return nil
885	}
886	
887	// invalidBracketedHost builds the content error for a bracketed host whose
888	// content is not a legal IPv6 literal.
889	func invalidBracketedHost(label, literal string) *Failure {
890		return failuref("invalid_config",
891			"%s: upstream host in brackets must be a valid IPv6 address, but %q is not a legal IPv6 address", label, literal)
892	}
893	
894	// validateUnbracketedUpstreamHost checks the split raw upstream's
895	// authority-without-brackets (hostPort) against the authority grammar:
896	//
897	//	host = IP-literal / IPv4address / reg-name
898	//	IP-literal = "[" ( IPv6address / ... ) "]"
899	//
900	// An unbracketed host part may therefore carry at most one colon, the one
901	// separating the host from its port:
902	//
903	//	reg-name [ ":" port ]
904	//
905	// Two or more colons are illegal no matter what the bytes spell: a bare IPv6
906	// literal leaves the host/port boundary undefined (the reader cannot tell
907	// "::1" from "::1:8080" with a port) and must be written as "[2001:db8::1]",
908	// while a name such as "api:internal:8080" or even a malformed IPv6-shaped
909	// spelling such as "2001:db8:::1" is not rescued by a numeric last segment —
910	// an extra colon stays an extra colon whether or not the address parses as
911	// IPv6 and whether or not a base path follows. The spelling is rejected on
912	// the colon count alone: the host and port are never guessed apart, brackets
913	// are never inserted and a trailing run of digits is never promoted to a
914	// port, so validity never depends on this Go release's url.Parse port
915	// strictness.
916	//
917	// When the part does parse as an IPv6 literal as written, the reason keeps
918	// the existing missing-brackets wording; a part that is merely
919	// multi-colon gets the extra-colon wording. The decision never strips a
920	// trailing ":<digits>" segment as a hypothetical port: every true bare IPv6
921	// spelling already parses whole ("::1:8080" and "fe80::1:8443" are complete
922	// addresses, whose last hextet merely happens to be digits), so stripping
923	// would only mislabel a malformed spelling such as "2001:db8:::1" that
924	// parses once a hextet is removed. Both reasons cover every form — the full
925	// form, the compressed form ("::1"), an IPv6 address with an embedded IPv4
926	// tail ("::ffff:192.0.2.1") and a percent-encoded zone ("%25eth0") — and
927	// both name the route's 1-based position, its id and the upstream field.
928	//
929	// Ordinary domains and bare IPv4 hosts (with or without a port) stay
930	// untouched, and the colons in userinfo or the base path are never
931	// inspected: only hostPort — the authority after the last '@' and before
932	// the first '/' according to the shared splitUpstream boundaries — is
933	// considered. Like the bracketed-host rule this is a content error in a
934	// syntactically valid JSON document, never a JSON parse failure, and it is
935	// decided on the raw bytes before url.Parse so the wording cannot regress to
936	// that parser's generic "invalid port" error.
937	func validateUnbracketedUpstreamHost(p upstreamParts, loc, id string) *Failure {
938		if p.schemeEnd < 0 {
939			return nil // no scheme: the generic absolute-URL check reports this
940		}
941		hostPort := p.hostPort
942		if hostPort == "" || strings.ContainsAny(hostPort, "[]") {
943			// No host (the generic check reports it) or a bracketed literal,
944			// which the bracketed-host validator owns.
945			return nil
946		}
947	
948		// A single colon is the legal host/port separator ("host:8080"); zero
949		// colons is a bare host. Count raw colons only: percent-encoded colons
950		// ("%3A") carry no separator byte, and userinfo and the base path were
951		// sliced off by splitUpstream.
952		if strings.Count(hostPort, ":") <= 1 {
953			return nil
954		}
955		label := routeLabel(loc, id)
956	
957		// Classify the spelling as written, never guessing a host/port split:
958		// percent-decode once so a "%25eth0" zone reaches netip as "%eth0" while
959		// every other byte keeps its spelling, then parse the whole hostPort. A
960		// legal IPv6 literal keeps the existing missing-brackets reason (this
961		// covers every form, "::1:8080" and "fe80::1:8443" included — a trailing
962		// hextet of digits is part of the address, not a guessed port); anything
963		// else that merely carries extra colons gets the extra-colon reason.
964		decoded, err := url.PathUnescape(hostPort)
965		if err == nil {
966			if addr, perr := netip.ParseAddr(decoded); perr == nil && addr.Is6() {
967				return failuref("invalid_config",
968					"%s: upstream IPv6 host %q is missing its square brackets: an IPv6 literal must be enclosed in a pair of brackets with any port outside them (e.g. \"[2001:db8::1]:8080\"); brackets are never added and a trailing number is not guessed as a port",
969					label, hostPort)
970			}
971		}
972		return failuref("invalid_config",
973			"%s: upstream %q has an unbracketed host part %q with more than one colon: a host without square brackets may contain at most the one colon separating it from its port (e.g. \"example.com:8080\"); an IPv6 literal must be enclosed in brackets (e.g. \"[2001:db8::1]:8080\") and the host and port are never guessed apart",
974			label, p.raw, hostPort)
975	}
976	
977	// invalidBracketedHostShape builds the content error for a bracketed host
978	// whose trailing bytes break the "single '[' IPv6 ']' pair plus optional
979	// port" grammar, e.g. a repeated bracket group, a stray closing bracket or
980	// non-port text after the closing bracket.
981	func invalidBracketedHostShape(label, suffix string) *Failure {
982		return failuref("invalid_config",
983			"%s: upstream bracketed host must be a single '[' IPv6 address ']' pair followed only by an optional port, but %q follows the closing ']'", label, suffix)
984	}

986	// requestJSON mirrors Request but keeps method and target raw, so a valid
987	// JSON document whose fields merely have the wrong JSON type is reported on
988	// the offending field instead of as a generic JSON decode error.
989	type requestJSON struct {
990		Method json.RawMessage `json:"method"`
991		Target json.RawMessage `json:"target"`
992	}
993	
994	// ParseRequest parses and validates one JSON request. Three failure shapes are
995	// kept apart: a document whose JSON syntax is broken fails as a parse failure
996	// without guessing a field; a syntactically valid non-object document (array,
997	// number, string, boolean or null) must be a JSON object; a valid object whose
998	// method or target is not a string fails on that field, naming the JSON type
999	// actually received (null counts as a type error, never as a missing field).
1000	// method is always checked before target, regardless of the key order in the
1001	// object. Only after both fields are present strings are their contents
1002	// (required method, legal token, absolute target without a fragment, a bad
1003	// percent escape, or a direct space/control character) validated, so an empty
1004	// string stays a content error.
1005	func ParseRequest(data []byte) (*Request, *Failure) {
1006		body, err := unmarshalJSONValue(data)
1007		if err != nil {
1008			return nil, failuref("invalid_request", "request is not valid JSON: %v", err)
1009		}
1010		if f := requireJSONObject(body, "invalid_request", "request", false); f != nil {
1011			return nil, f
1012		}
1013	
1014		var rj requestJSON
1015		if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &rj); err != nil {
1016			// The document already parsed as one JSON value and starts with '{';
1017			// keep this as a parse failure rather than a field error if the object
1018			// itself cannot be read.
1019			return nil, failuref("invalid_request", "request is not valid JSON: %v", err)
1020		}
1021	
1022		var req Request
1023		// method is always checked before target, regardless of the key order in
1024		// the object; the absent/null/non-string distinction is the shared
1025		// decodeStringField, so only the request wording is added here.
1026		if f := decodeRequestStringField(rj.Method, "method", &req.Method); f != nil {
1027			return nil, f
1028		}
1029		if f := decodeRequestStringField(rj.Target, "target", &req.Target); f != nil {
1030			return nil, f
1031		}
1032	
1033		switch {
1034		case req.Method == "":
1035			return nil, failuref("invalid_request", "method is required")
1036		case !isToken(req.Method):
1037			return nil, failuref("invalid_request", "method %q is not a legal HTTP method", req.Method)
1038		}
1039		switch {
1040		case req.Target == "" || req.Target[0] != '/':
1041			return nil, failuref("invalid_request", "target must start with /")
1042		case strings.Contains(req.Target, "#"):
1043			return nil, failuref("invalid_request", "target must not contain a fragment")
1044		case !validPercentEscapes(req.Target):
1045			return nil, failuref("invalid_request", "target contains an invalid percent escape")
1046		}
1047		if f := validateTargetCharacters(req.Target); f != nil {
1048			return nil, f
1049		}
1050		return &req, nil
1051	}
1052	
1053	// decodeRequestStringField renders the request wording for one string field;
1054	// the absent/null/non-string decision itself is the shared
1055	// decodeStringField. An absent field (no such key) is left as the zero value
1056	// so the later content checks keep their "field is required" behavior; null
1057	// or any non-string JSON value is a type error that names the field and the
1058	// JSON type that was actually supplied.
1059	func decodeRequestStringField(raw json.RawMessage, field string, dst *string) *Failure {
1060		if !decodeStringField(raw, dst) {
1061			return failuref("invalid_request", "%s must be a string, got %s", field, jsonTypeName(raw))
1062		}
1063		return nil
1064	}
1065	
1066	// jsonTypeName names the JSON type of a syntactically valid raw value, in the
1067	// terms the request error reasons use: "null", "a boolean", "a number",
1068	// "a string", "an array" or "an object".
1069	func jsonTypeName(raw json.RawMessage) string {
1070		switch bytes.TrimSpace(raw)[0] {
1071		case 'n':
1072			return "null"
1073		case 't', 'f':
1074			return "a boolean"
1075		case '"':
1076			return "a string"
1077		case '[':
1078			return "an array"
1079		case '{':
1080			return "an object"
1081		default:
1082			return "a number"
1083		}
1084	}

1086	// Resolve matches a validated request against a validated configuration and
1087	// computes the upstream URL. Failure codes are route_not_found and
1088	// route_conflict.
1089	func Resolve(cfg *Config, req *Request) (*Resolution, *Failure) {
1090		// Reject a target carrying a direct space or control character before
1091		// route selection, conflict resolution and query rewriting, so such a
1092		// request can never match a prefix (and carry the byte into
1093		// upstreamURL), report a conflict, or have a remove/set hide the
1094		// offending parameter. ParseRequest already ran this check; it is
1095		// repeated here so a request built in-process cannot bypass it.
1096		if f := validateTargetCharacters(req.Target); f != nil {
1097			return nil, f
1098		}
1099		path := req.Target
1100		if i := strings.IndexByte(path, '?'); i >= 0 {
1101			path = path[:i]
1102		}
1103	
1104		type candidate struct {
1105			route    *Route
1106			concrete bool
1107		}
1108		var matched []candidate
1109		for i := range cfg.Routes {
1110			route := &cfg.Routes[i]
1111			concrete, wildcard := methodMatch(route.Methods, req.Method)
1112			if !concrete && !wildcard {
1113				continue
1114			}
1115			if !prefixMatch(route.PathPrefix, path) {
1116				continue
1117			}
1118			matched = append(matched, candidate{route, concrete})
1119		}
1120		if len(matched) == 0 {
1121			return nil, failuref("route_not_found", "no route matches %s %s", req.Method, path)
1122		}
1123	
1124		// Longest prefix wins.
1125		bestLen := 0
1126		for _, c := range matched {
1127			if n := len(c.route.PathPrefix); n > bestLen {
1128				bestLen = n
1129			}
1130		}
1131		winners := matched[:0]
1132		for _, c := range matched {
1133			if len(c.route.PathPrefix) == bestLen {
1134				winners = append(winners, c)
1135			}
1136		}
1137	
1138		// Among equal prefixes a concrete method beats the wildcard.
1139		var concrete []candidate
1140		for _, c := range winners {
1141			if c.concrete {
1142				concrete = append(concrete, c)
1143			}
1144		}
1145		if len(concrete) > 0 {
1146			winners = concrete
1147		}
1148		if len(winners) > 1 {
1149			ids := make([]string, 0, len(winners))
1150			for _, c := range winners {

All done. The regression coverage is in place and verified.

## What was added

New file `contractsentinel/query_copy_regression_test.go` — six test functions that exercise the public path (`ParseConfig` → `ParseRequest` → `Resolve`, plus save/reload via `json.Marshal`/`ParseConfig`), mirroring the conventions of the existing `query_remove_regression_test.go`:

- **`TestQueryTransformCopyComplexSeparatorName`** — copying `a&b=c` → `x=y&z`: both `a%26b%3dc` and `a%26b%3Dc` hit (hex case irrelevant); each source gets exactly one copy placed immediately after itself; sources keep their original name encoding, position and value; the new name is written `x%3Dy%26z`; pre-existing `x=y&z` parameters stay put, unmerged and unoverwritten. Also pins: first-`=` split with raw value bytes preserved verbatim (`+`, mixed-case escapes, extra `=`), valueless source → valueless copy, empty value keeps its `=`, non-hit parameters and empty fragments keep bytes/order, `a=b=1` is named `a` so a rule named `a=b` (or `a&b=c`) cannot hit it, decoded-name case sensitivity, and no-hit/no-query/empty-`?` cases.
- **`TestQueryTransformCopyLiteralEncodingSemantics`** — request names are decoded exactly once, rule names are literal: a rule named `%26` copies `%2526` but not `%26`; copying *to* the literal `%26` writes the copy as `%2526` (never a separator, never merged with an existing `%26` parameter); literal `%` and `&` source names likewise.
- **`TestQueryTransformCopyComplexNameChainRemove`** — copy `a&b=c` → `x=y&z` followed by remove `x=y&z` deletes both the fresh copies and the originally target-named parameters, while sources survive with their original encodings, positions and values.
- **`TestQueryTransformCopyComplexNameKeepsRoutingAndJoin`** — `routeId` and upstream path joining are untouched by the rule; a transform-free route keeps the same query byte for byte.
- **`TestQueryTransformCopyComplexNameInvalidEscapeNoPartialSuccess`** — incomplete/non-hex escapes in request names (before/after/inside the copied parameter, valued or valueless) return `invalid_request` from both `ParseRequest` and a `ParseRequest`-bypassing `Resolve`, even with a later remove rule in the chain, and never leave a partial `Resolution`.
- **`TestQueryTransformCopyComplexNameRoundTrip`** — the special-character rules survive a save/reload literally and in order (only JSON string escaping on save), and the same request resolves identically before and after.

## Verification

- `go test ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `go test -race` — all pass; `gofmt` clean.
- Mutation-checked the new tests: double-decoding the rule's source name and appending copies at the end instead of after each source both make the new tests fail, confirming they guard the pinned semantics. Production code was restored untouched (`git status` shows only the new test file).
